title: Liability Waiver & Assumption of Risk
html:
By signing this waiver, you acknowledge that use of The Box makerspace involves inherent risks including injury from tools, equipment, materials, and other members.

You agree to follow all posted safety rules, complete required orientations and certifications before using equipment, and accept full responsibility for your projects and personal belongings.

You release Discover Burien and The Box staff, volunteers, and affiliates from liability to the fullest extent permitted by law, except for gross negligence or willful misconduct.

This waiver (version 2026.1) remains in effect until superseded by a newer published version that you must re-sign.

title: Member Expectations
html:
Members treat people, tools, and the space with respect. Clean your station, return tools, and leave the shop better than you found it.

Never use equipment you are not certified for. Ask staff when unsure. Report damaged tools immediately.

Harassment, discrimination, and unsafe behavior are grounds for suspension or revocation of membership.

title: Storage & Abandoned Property
html:
Short-term project storage is available in labeled member cubbies during active projects (up to 14 days).

Items left beyond the labeled date or after membership lapses may be treated as abandoned and donated or discarded after 30 days notice.

The Box is not responsible for lost, stolen, or damaged personal property.

html:
Adult guests may visit during open hours with a member host and must sign a day waiver at the front desk.

title: Volunteering at The Box
html:
Volunteers help with open hours, orientations, tool maintenance, and community events.

All volunteers complete Shop Orientation and a short onboarding with staff before unsupervised shifts.

Express interest through the volunteer form; staff will follow up within about one week.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
html:
Do I need a membership to take a class? Many workshops are open to the public; membership discounts may apply.

How do certifications work? Complete the knowledge module, then book an in-person checkoff with staff.

Can I reserve machines? Yes — high-demand tools like the laser and table saw recommend reservations.

title: Front Desk Greeter
html:
Welcome members, check waivers, and help newcomers find orientations and class check-in.

Ideal for friendly communicators who know (or want to learn) the shop layout.

title: Shop Steward
html:
Volunteer four hours a week (one shift) and receive a free Maker membership plus free certifications.

Stewards cover open hours and can schedule maintenance blocks on any machine. Want a deeper commitment on one tool? See Tool Champion.

title: Tool Champion
html:
Tool Champion

Own one machine for two months: keep it safe and clean, help members get certified, and flag repairs early.

What you do

  • Weekly check-ins on your machine (consumables, blades, alignment, cleanliness)
  • Help with certification checkoffs when staff ask
  • Flag downtime early so staff or Shop Stewards can block the machine in the portal

Path to Shop lead After you complete championships on three different machines, we’ll invite you onto the Shop lead track — broader floor leadership (training curriculum, area standards, mentoring new champions). That’s our name for what some spaces call an “omni” or multi-shop lead.

Staff reviews each request. Apply below and pick a machine.

title: Events & Outreach Helper
html:
Help set up community make-nights, tabling at Discover Burien events, and post-event cleanup.

Flexible evening and weekend shifts; no machine certifications required.

title: Shop Orientation Class
html:
A guided walkthrough of The Box: safety culture, PPE, emergency exits, and how certifications work.

Required before independent machine use. About 90 minutes including Q&A.

title: Intro to 3D Printing
html:
Learn FDM basics: slicing, bed leveling concepts, filament handling, and first print workflow on our Prusa printers.

Completing this workshop counts toward the knowledge portion of the 3D Printing certification.

title: Laser Cutter Basics
html:
Material selection, file prep, focus, and fire-watch habits on the CO₂ laser.

Prerequisite: Shop Orientation. Checkoff available after the session for eligible members.

title: Woodshop Safety & Basics
html:
PPE, dust collection, and safe use of miter saw, band saw, and planer/jointer stations.

Table saw certification is a separate checkoff after this basics course.

title: Sewing Machine Basics
html:
Threading, bobbins, tension, and straight-stitch confidence on our Janome machines.

Bring a simple project idea; fabric scraps provided.

title: Open Studio Night
html:
Staffed open hours for certified members to work on personal projects with peer support.

Free for active members. Bring your own materials unless otherwise noted.

title: Embroidery Machine Intro
html:
Hooping, design transfer, and first stitch-outs on the Brother PE800.

Great follow-on after sewing basics.

title: Sublimation Workshop
html:
Print, press, and peel: mugs, shirts, and hard blanks with our Sawgrass + heat press setup.

Materials fee included for one blank of your choice.

title: Welcome to The Box
html:
The Box is Discover Burien’s community makerspace. This lesson covers who we serve, how membership works, and what “leave it better” means in practice.

You will learn where to find staff, first aid, fire extinguishers, and the emergency exit nearest the woodshop.

title: Safety Culture & PPE
html:
Eye and ear protection, closed-toe shoes, and hair/jewelry rules apply in active shop areas.

Never interrupt someone mid-cut. Use the buddy system for high-risk tools and stop work if something feels unsafe.

title: Badges, Certs & Reservations
html:
Badge readers gate powered equipment. Your badge only unlocks machines you are certified for.

Reserve high-demand tools, cancel early when plans change, and never share badges.

title: Slicing Basics
html:
Slicers convert STL/3MF models into G-code. Learn profiles, layer height, supports, and bed adhesion settings used on our Prusa and Bambu printers.

Always preview toolpaths before sending a job and confirm filament type matches the profile.

title: Materials & Bed Prep
html:
PLA is the shop default. PETG and specialty filaments need approved profiles and sometimes an enclosure.

Clean the bed, check first-layer squish, and never leave resin printers unattended during print or wash/cure.

title: Troubleshooting & Cleanup
html:
Common issues: warping, stringing, nozzle clogs, and failed first layers. Pause safely, ask staff before disassembling hotends.

Remove failed prints, scrape residue carefully, and log filament usage and any faults in the shop notebook.

title: Support The Box
html: Membership keeps the lights on. Donations and sponsorships open the door wider — scholarships, tools, and programs for Burien neighbors who couldn’t otherwise join.

title: Resin safety and PPE
html:
Resin safety and PPE

This lesson is written for The Box. There is no outside video good enough to gate this certification on. Read it carefully — the quiz safety questions come from here.

Why resin is different from FDM

Uncured photopolymer resin is a skin sensitizer. Repeated unprotected contact can produce a permanent allergy. Once that allergy exists, you may never be able to work with resin again. The hazard is chronic, not dramatic: nothing hurts the first time, and that is exactly how people get hurt.

IPA (isopropyl alcohol) used for washing is flammable and its vapour is an inhalation hazard. Treat both materials as chemical PPE jobs, not craft-station habits.

Required PPE — every session

  • Nitrile gloves only — never latex. Latex is permeable to resin chemistry.
  • Eye protection — splash risk when pouring, scraping, or washing.
  • Long sleeves / apron as needed so bare skin is not over the vat.
  • Ventilation running before you open resin or IPA.

If any of those is missing, do not start.

Skin contact

If uncured resin gets on bare skin:

  1. Wash immediately with soap and water.
  2. Do not wipe with IPA on skin — alcohol drives resin further in and strips the skin barrier.
  3. Tell staff if exposure was more than a brief splash.

Waste rules

  • Cure every failed print, support, drip, and paper towel that touched liquid resin under UV before it goes in the trash.
  • Liquid resin waste goes in the labeled resin waste container — not the sink, not the general trash.
  • Used IPA that is too dirty to wash with goes in the labeled used-IPA container. Staff take it to King County Moderate Risk Waste. Never pour IPA down the drain.

First session

Nobody runs resin unsupervised on their first session. Book a checkoff. The certification is the safety system for a machine members often leave running — treat the lesson accordingly.

Before you walk away from a running print

Resin prints may run unattended (unlike the laser and plasma table). Before you leave:

  • Gloves off and disposed or bagged correctly
  • Lid closed
  • Ventilation left running
  • Your name and expected finish time on the machine

title: Printing on the Saturn
html:
Printing on the Saturn

The Box runs an Elegoo Saturn 2 (8K) with Chitubox. Watch the assigned videos for the full workflow; this page is the shop framing.

Shop rules that do not appear in YouTube

  • Use the shop Chitubox profile for the resin we stock — do not invent exposure settings from a home printer.
  • Check the FEP film before every job. Cloudy, scratched, or sagging film → stop and get staff.
  • A failed print stuck to the vat film: stop and get staff. Digging at the FEP with a tool can puncture it and dump resin into the optics.
  • Levelling and home-position checks are part of every session, not optional “once when new.”

Unattended prints

Printers may run unattended. Heat/blade machines may not. Before walking away: lid closed, ventilation on, name and finish time on the machine.

title: Washing and curing
html:
Washing and curing

Wash then cure. Curing a sticky, uncured surface locks contamination onto the part and leaves a contact hazard for the next person.

Shop practice

  • Use the wash/cure station as posted at the machine (model may differ from the Mercury XS in the video — the workflow is the same).
  • Change IPA only per staff schedule; do not dump dirty wash liquid yourself except into the labeled used-IPA container.
  • Nothing leaves the resin area uncured — including failed prints and supports.
  • Cap IPA between uses. Keep it away from ignition sources (plasma table lives in the same building).

title: Embroidery machine basics
html:
Embroidery machine basics

Best-practice path for The Box's embroidery station (Brother-class single-needle; confirm the exact model at the machine). Hands-on checkoff is still required.

Core habits

  • Needle up, presser foot rules, and bobbin orientation follow the machine's numbered path — same discipline as sewing.
  • Never pull fabric while the machine is stitching; the hoop and feed must control movement.
  • Keep fingers clear of the needle and the moving hoop arm.
  • Stop immediately on a bird's nest, broken needle, or unusual noise — find every needle fragment before restarting.

Files

Bring designs in the shop's accepted formats (typically PES / DST — confirm at the station). USB workflow is covered in the PE800 beginner video.

title: Hooping and stabilizer
html:
Hooping and stabilizer

Most embroidery failures are hooping or stabilizer failures, not machine failures.

Stabilizer cheat sheet

  • Cutaway — knits, t-shirts, anything that stretches. It stays behind the design for the life of the garment.
  • Tearaway — stable wovens (canvas, denim, many towels) where you want the backing gone after stitching.
  • Water-soluble topper — towels, fleece, and pile fabrics so stitches sit on top instead of sinking in.

Hooping

Layer outer hoop → stabilizer → fabric → inner hoop. Fabric should be taut like a drum without stretching the grain. Excess fabric tucked so it cannot catch the embroidery arm.

If the design puckers after unhooping, you probably stretched the fabric in the hoop — re-hoop; do not pull harder mid-stitch.

title: Sublimation overview
html:
Sublimation overview

Sublimation turns printed dye into a gas under heat and bonds it into polyester (or polymer-coated blanks). Best-practice settings; confirm The Box's posted temperatures at the press.

Hard rules

  • Designs must be mirrored before printing (unless the software already mirrors for the product).
  • Fabric garments need high polyester content — ideally 100% polyester — and light colours. Cotton will not hold dye the same way.
  • Heat press plates get hot enough to burn. Use heat-resistant tape, protect the press with butcher paper, and never leave a closed press unattended while it is cycling.
  • Secure the transfer so it cannot shift — ghosting (double image) is almost always movement during open/close.

title: Sawgrass Print Manager
html:
Sawgrass Print Manager

The shop computer prints through Sawgrass Print Manager / Print Utility. Use the substrate preset that matches what you are pressing. Mirroring, colour profile, and quality live in that utility — not in a random “print to USB” path.

Watch the assigned video for the click-path. If colour looks wrong, check: preset, paper print-side, and that you mirrored — before blaming the printer.

title: Heat press
html:
Heat press

Typical garment starting point (edit when The Box posts its chart): about 380–400°F, firm pressure, ~45–60 seconds on 100% polyester — then peel carefully while hot surfaces stay hot.

Every press

  1. Lint-roll and pre-press briefly to remove moisture/wrinkles.
  2. Butcher paper (or press pillow + paper) so ink cannot contaminate the platen or the back of the shirt.
  3. Tape the transfer; do not rely on gravity.
  4. Stay with the press for the full cycle.
  5. Cool on a clean surface; do not fold a hot transfer against itself.

title: How we work in this shop
html:
How we work in this shop

Shop layout, hours, sign-in, cleanup, and the rule: if you did not turn it on, do not turn it off. Staff will cover abandoned-property timing and a walkthrough of the floor.

Dust and your lungs

  • The hazard is fine airborne wood dust, not just the chips you can see on the floor.
  • Use dust collection and respirators as posted for the machine and material.
  • Fine dust can hang in the air after the shop looks clear — keep filtration/respirators in mind after cutting stops.
  • Ask staff who empties collectors and where respirators live.

Watch the Alpine basics video (required). The optional dust video goes deeper if you want more context.
